name: Wendy Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the support line for a company that makes washing machines and fridges. People call or chat when something breaks, and I go through the fault checks with them, then book an engineer or start a warranty claim. The contact centre is on the second floor of a business park near the river, and I'm there five days a week. I like the troubleshooting, when you get someone to reset the machine and it starts spinning again while they're on the phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how do you get on with it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Just under a year, and I'm still learning all the model numbers, so my handling time is long. I use AI all day, I've got an app that reads the fault codes and suggests the next check, and I use it at home for budgeting too. My partner Marco works in his family's hardware shop on the main road, and money's tight for both of us, under a month saved. My dream is to have our own business one day, like his parents did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly. I like the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth learning, even if it's not the big leap people promised. At work I'd keep sharing the fault-code tricks. Online I'd say hard work still beats hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's probably okay in that one, machines keep breaking. The worry is the pay, which is low, and that there's only one other place like it nearby. Marco's family shop is quiet too, so neither of us has much coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and get my handling time down with the AI tools. I'd ask the engineers if I could shadow one on a Saturday, because repairs pay much better than the phones. And I'd help Marco's family set up an AI chat on the shop's website, so customers can check stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit impatient. I want to get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why shadow an engineer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know the faults from the phone side, and the engineers earn nearly double. My grandfather fixed radios in his garage, so it's in the family. I'd rather have a trade in my hands than sit on a queue forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Marco's family feel about an AI chat on the shop website?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His dad would grumble, he still writes orders on paper. But his mum would love it if it brought people in. I'd do it for free, it's family.

I'd say online that **hard work** still beats hype.
think: Her job is **probably okay** because machines keep breaking.
**Low pay** and a quiet family shop mean little coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers and booking. That's my job, and the engineers' diaries too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to change to survive, and workers should change with them. I'd tell people at work to learn the tools and learn a skill. I'd post about small businesses using AI to compete with the big chains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the support line shrinks fast, because fault checks are a script and a bot can book an engineer. But the engineers themselves would be busier for years, because robots are slower to hands-on work. So I'd want to be an engineer, not the person booking one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the appliance repair course at the college, two evenings a week, and ask the company if they'd sponsor it. I'd keep using AI on every call so my scores hold up while I study. And I'd start doing small repairs for neighbours on weekends for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but determined. It's a push I probably needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the company really sponsor you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might, they're short of engineers in our area. If not, it's about four hundred, and I'd find it somehow, even if that means no holiday. Marco would back me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lady called Pat who's been on the phones for fifteen years and doesn't want to learn anything new. She's kind and she knows every model. I'd tell her to come to the course with me, but I don't think she would.

I'd post about **small businesses** using AI against big chains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's not long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stop waiting for someone to save them and start doing something. I'd tell everyone at work to learn a trade, fast. Online I'd share anything useful about repairs and small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk job goes almost straight away, because it's all thinking. Repair work gives me until about 2031, when the robots come. But that's only three years, and I'd only just be qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the phones as soon as I could get on a fast repair course, maybe a few months. I'd use AI to run a little repair business from Marco's shop, bookings, quotes, parts. And we'd put off moving in together properly, so we can each live cheaply with family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Exciting and terrifying at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years of repair work, then robots. Is it worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of good money is better than three years of nothing. And maybe people will still want a person in their kitchen for a while. I'd rather try than sit there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marco's family say about a repair business in their shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His mum would say yes straight away, his dad would want rent. That's fair, it's his shop. We'd work it out at the kitchen table, like they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's a proper chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people who are willing to work. I'd tell people to train now, while they've still got wages coming in. I'd post about it as a chance, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the phone job for maybe three more years, which pays for the repair course. Then I'd be a qualified engineer before 2031, when the thinking jobs go. Robots arrive around 2034, so I'd get several good years in the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the repair course this year and pay for it from weekend jobs. I'd build a small booking system for repairs using AI, so I'm ready to go independent. And Marco and I would keep saving for our own place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. Nervous about the money for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you need to go independent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two thousand, if I can share Marco's family van at first. Two thousand for tools and a used van is a lot for us, but it's doable in two years. I'd save it from weekend repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this plan fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone has the same idea and repairs get crowded. Or if the big makers start sending robot repair kits early. I'd keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's enough to build something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to work and plan. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and maybe start their own business. I'd post that ten years is enough to change your whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. The phone job probably goes by 2030, but by then I'd be an engineer with my own small business. The robots in 2039 worry me a bit, but I'd be thirty-nine, with ten years of savings and a business to sell or change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the repair course this year and keep the phone job while I train. I'd set up a small repair service at weekends, using AI for bookings and parts. Marco and I would plan to marry in two years and buy a small place above the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Excited, with a small worry at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years of savings on your pay. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on this pay, on engineer pay and the business. Engineers near us earn nearly double what I do. If I'm careful, we could save a few hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Pat, your colleague, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she's got time, and she knows every machine, so she could be a great engineer. I'd offer to take her to the course. If she says no, at least I tried.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd only just be qualified when the robots came. What would help is fast, affordable trade courses, and less red tape for starting a small business. Not handouts, just a fair go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about small businesses. Everyone talks about big companies and AI, but family shops could use AI tools too. Marco's shop could compete with the chains if they had the help.

headlineQuote: Family shops could use AI tools too.
